title: The centurion's faith (Luke 7:1–10)
hookLine: a Roman officer says: just say the word
last: OUT OF THE HEART THE MOUTH SPEAKS.

lines: THE ELDERS: HE BUILT US A SYNAGOGUE.
cards: A centurion was a military officer, and this one is not Jewish: an unlikely person at the center of a story about faith in a small Jewish town.

In Capernaum, Luke says, his servant is dying, a servant "who was dear unto him." The first surprise: the centurion doesn't go to Jesus himself. He sends the elders of the Jewish community, and they plead his case warmly.
He's worthy, they say: "For he loveth our nation, and he hath built us a synagogue." A foreign officer, and the town's elders are his advocates.

teach.b: So Jesus goes with them. When he's nearly at the house, the centurion sends friends with a message.
In the King James words: "Lord, trouble not thyself: for I am not worthy that thou shouldest enter under my roof." The elders said he's worthy. He says I'm not.
A man who gives orders to soldiers, telling a traveling teacher, don't trouble yourself with me.

teach.h: A MAN UNDER AUTHORITY: SAY THE WORD.
teach.b: Then he explains why Jesus needn't come at all: "say in a word, and my servant shall be healed. For I also am a man set under authority, having under me soldiers, and I say unto one, Go, and he goeth; and to another, Come, and he cometh."
He knows a word from the right person is enough, no matter the distance. Luke says Jesus "marvelled at him." This time Jesus is the one amazed.
He turns to the crowd: "I say unto you, I have not found so great faith, no, not in Israel." When the friends get back to the house, the servant is well.

teach.h: THEY NEVER MEET FACE TO FACE.
teach.b: In Luke's version, the centurion and Jesus never meet face to face; the whole story happens through messengers, and a word sent across a distance.

teach.h: SAY IN A WORD, AND MY SERVANT SHALL BE HEALED.
teach.b: Catholics echo the centurion at Mass: just before communion, the people say they are not worthy for the Lord to come under their roof, but ask him only to say the word.
An officer's message, still spoken in churches today.

how: At Catholic Mass, just before communion, the congregation says a form of the centurion's words, saying they are not worthy for the Lord to enter under their roof and asking him only to say the word.

games.q: you're a Roman officer. the teacher you asked for is almost at your door. what do you do?
o: meet him at the gate with honor.
send friends: don't trouble yourself; only say the word.
send soldiers to hurry him along.
games.why: the centurion sends word that he isn't worthy to have Jesus under his roof, and that a word is enough. Jesus marvels at his faith.

practice: Bring to mind someone you can't easily reach right now, a friend in another city, someone in a hospital bed or a hard season.
Find a word short enough to fit in one breath, thinking of you, I'm here, and say it slowly in your mind, as if it were already on its way.
If you pray, you can echo the centurion and ask God only to say the word for them; if you don't, simply hold the word and the person together.

wordCard.voice: Centurion. An officer who says he isn't worthy to have Jesus under his roof, and trusts that one word, sent from a distance, is enough.

orig.note: Greek: commander of a hundred, a centurion.

carryVoice: Your line: only say the word. A word can travel where you can't. That's day five hundred twenty-six.
